quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

agent_returns.text:
**Edges:** census — household record (both 1870 and 1880). No new relationship edges needed: the Couple (I1-I2) and ParentChild (I1/I2 → I3, I4, I5) relationships already exist in the tree, sourced from the English 1851/1861 census records; this Tennessee evidence corroborates those existing edges rather than creating new ones.

**Household check (1870, src_001):** wife Mary — present as household_member_1; children James, Ellen, George — all present as household_member_2/3/4. Full match to the tree's known family of four plus parents.

**Household check (1880, src_002):** wife Mary — present as wife; George — present as son; **James — absent; Ellen — absent** (neither has a `diedByYear`, so nothing rules them out — by 1880 James would be ~28 and Ellen ~25, consistent with having left the parental home, married, or been enumerated elsewhere; this is flagged as an open identity question, not resolved here).

**Geographic-plausibility cap:** The nearest tree-attested residence before this run is Horsham, Sussex, England (1861). Both census households place the family in Maury County, Tennessee — 6,804 km away. The FamilySearch "Tennessee Emigration and Immigration" wiki page names no arrival corridor from England for this household's era, and no passenger list, naturalization record, or other documentary bridge exists in the project. Per policy this caps every link tied to this unexplained transatlantic move at `probable`, never `confident`, regardless of how strong the other correlation is.

**Coherence dry-run:** `merge_warnings` against a candidate record document was not run — only pre-extracted assertions were available for src_001/src_002 (no `record_read` document retained), so the gate was skipped as the skill allows; cross-person consistency was instead checked by hand (head/spouse/children map correctly in both years) and found coherent.

**Links created (22 `pe_` entries, pe_001–pe_022), all `probable`, `match_score` 0.78:**

| Record | Person | Entries |
|---|---|---|
| 1870 (src_001) | William Weller (I1) | pe_001, pe_002, pe_011 (name/birth/residence) |
| 1870 | Mary Weller (I2) | pe_003, pe_004 |
| 1870 | James Weller (I3) | pe_005, pe_006 |
| 1870 | Ellen Weller (I4) | pe_007, pe_008 |
| 1870 | George Weller (I5) | pe_009, pe_010 |
| 1880 (src_002) | William Weller (I1) | pe_012, pe_013, pe_018, pe_020 (name/birth/residence + both relationship assertions naming him) |
| 1880 | Mary Weller (I2) | pe_014, pe_015, pe_019 |
| 1880 | George Weller (I5) | pe_016, pe_017, pe_021 |

Every name/age/residence identifier agrees exactly across both censuses and the English record baseline (ages progress correctly by exactly 10 years between 1870 and 1880, and are consistent with the 1825/1828/1859 birth years already on file); only the unexplained Atlantic crossing kept these at `probable` rather than `confident`. `materialize_facts` then wrote the 1870 and 1880 facts onto I1, I2, I3, I4 and I5 with no conflicts surfaced. `person_warnings` on all five pre-existing persons returned only pre-existing, low-severity "non-standard place" notices (a place-formatting issue, unrelated to this linking) — nothing chronological or relationship-wise was introduced.

---
Both the 1870 and 1880 Tennessee census pages for the William Weller household have now been tied to your William Weller, his wife Mary, and their children James, Ellen, and George — the names, ages (which tick up by exactly ten years between the two censuses, as they should), and family grouping all line up very well with what you already had on them from England. The one thing holding these links at "probably the same family" rather than "certainly" is that nothing yet explains how they got from Sussex, England to Tennessee — no immigration or ship record has turned up in your files, and the general history of English settlement in Tennessee doesn't point to that particular route, so that's a gap worth closing with more research. Also worth noting: in the 1880 census only George appears with his parents — James and Ellen are missing from that household, which is worth asking about (did they marry and move out, or were they just living elsewhere that year) rather than assuming anything. The next step would be to search for a passenger list, naturalization record, or similar document that shows the family's move from England to Tennessee, and separately to look for James and Ellen in other 1880-era records.
